column2: Albers invites the Swiss émigré Schawinsky (a student of Schlemmer's from 1924 to 1928) to teach painting and theater. Fleeing Nazi Germany, Schawinsky had passed through Italy and advertising. advertising clients: Illy Caffè, Cinzano vermouth, Olivetti typewriters; a widely circulated photomontage of Mussolini at the head of the masses for the 12th anniversary of the Fascist revolution Consequences: Schawinsky becomes the sole champion and interpreter of Bauhaus theater in the United States

Anni and Josef Albers visit Mexico, notably the archaeological site of Monte Alban; this encounter feeds Ancient Writing (gold threads, glyphs) and Monte Alban. gold threads in Ancient Writing; the stepped temples of Monte Alban Consequences: a mid-1930s turn toward symbolic imagery

The writer Louis Adamic, on a visit in 1936, takes down a long explanation from Rice: teaching method rather than content, process rather than results; education is not “obtained,” it is experienced; facts change, but the method of dealing with them remains; philosophy, literature, art, music, and dramatics are the best training grounds for the imagination. remarks published in “Education on a Mountain,” pp. 518-19 Consequences: the fullest statement of Rice's doctrine of art at the center of the curriculum

Three years after the opening, Locke — a former liberal colleague from Lincoln (Nebraska), now the fiercely independent editor of the Dayton Daily News — visits the college (~50 students, 16 teachers). Noticing that the close-knit original group is diversifying, he asks Rice what he will do when a schemer arrives. Rice, very self-assured, shrugs. He will later decide that the schemer — Irving Knickerbocker — was already there. about 50 students, 16 teachers Consequences: a foreboding of the conflicts to come

Rice calls a general meeting on the nature of institutions that blindly outlive their purposes, then asks why not decide, that very evening, to close the college so that it might become unique among all institutions. Silence, a hiccup, then debate; Rice ready with every argument, with the most powerful voice; a refugee from Central America, tortured in his country's prisons, rises and launches into a tirade with no direct bearing on the subject. The meeting fizzles out of its own accord; Rice remains seated at the end of the table, smoking his pipe, beside a tiny log cabin he has built out of his pipe matches. a tiny log cabin made of burnt matches, set at Rice's elbow; the Depression years; European refugees in the audience Consequences: a demonstration of Rice's ambivalence toward any institutional attachment

Before the Adamics leave, Louis reads his draft at a community meeting. The article salutes the pioneering students and singles out Albers and Wunsch, but above all puts Rice on a pedestal: an idealist-optimist, intelligent, well informed, fantastically honest, perhaps one of the great teachers of all time. The discussion that follows is critical: several students say for the first time that Rice is a sometimes insensitive Socrates whose power can be misused. Zeuch declares that Adamic, with no experience of community or education, was in fact ghostwritten by Rice. Adamic's remarks on Rice; the “open secret” of the ghostwriting Consequences: Rice admits to blunders and says he is hungry for recognition; the article attracts a wave of applications

After the warning, Rice advises Goldenson, a keen golfer and a good coach, to give up classroom teaching and become a professional golf instructor. At a faculty meeting (December 7, 1936), Goldenson cites this as proof of insensitivity; Dreier thinks it was very good advice; Wunsch mentions that Rice has also made insensitive remarks about his productions; Goldenson retorts: not after being dismissed from the faculty. Rice explains that his advice was calculated, to shock Goldenson out of the idea that one teaches with a mass of information. Consequences: Goldenson's growing resentment

Goldenson, backed by Zeuch and others, objects that no colleague had yet attended his classes when the written warning arrived in his mailbox. He was judged on peripheral things, he says, like judging a city by its suburbs. A warning received in his mailbox

Knickerbocker listens sympathetically to students (especially new and young ones) unhappy with the college and with Rice. Factions form, the students lining up behind Rice or Knickerbocker. Wunsch, seeing the community on the verge of splitting into two colleges, considers that Knickerbocker coddles the students; Dreier tends to agree. Knickerbocker says he must protect certain students from Rice's extremely destructive effect on personality, and claims to have given them all the information he could about Rice and his methods. Consequences: An internal cold-war climate; some hope for a quiet departure of both men during the summer, but both come back

De Kooning becomes friends with two neighbors: the writer and dance critic Edwin Denby and the photographer Rudolph Burckhardt, a descendant of the historian Jacob Burckhardt. They become his first collectors; Burckhardt's carefully composed black-and-white photographs shape the artist's public image.

De Kooning makes contact with the fledgling American Abstract Artists association, dominated by Communist ideas; his political sense ensures him rapid acceptance, but despite several invitations he refuses to become an official member: he cannot accept the group's prohibitions (notably on figuration) and remains interested in art as a whole, feeling himself an outsider, different. Consequences: He keeps his independence between abstraction and figuration.

Friendships with the photographer Rudolph Burckhardt and the poet and dance critic Edwin Denby, who become his first collectors; at Ibram Lassaw's, takes part in the discussions leading to the founding of the American Abstract Artists; meets Harold Rosenberg; devotes himself exclusively to painting and begins the series of standing and seated male figures; first participation in a group exhibition, “New Horizons in American Art” at MoMA.

Cubism and Abstract Art, then Fantastic Art, Dada and Surrealism, follow one another in the spring and winter of 1936, establishing the dual framework of abstract formal rigor and appeal to the unconscious in which Abstract Expressionism will be born. Consequences: A decisive impetus to de Kooning's abstract ventures, culminating in Elegy (c. 1939)

The Terramare office, the regime's official public relations body, commissions from Bayer a brochure distributed worldwide to extol the Führer's achievements. Cover: a young blond Aryan, smiling, serious, and proud, in Hitler Youth uniform, a German flag in hand; the photo playfully arranged, the typography emphasizing purity and verve. Consequences: One of Bayer's many brochures and posters for the Reich.

Bayer designs a brochure celebrating life in the Third Reich and Hitler's impact, accompanying an exhibition for tourists at the Berlin Olympics. He includes the Heinkel factory designed by Herbert Rimpl. Later, he will discuss only its duotone technique. A brochure with the Heinkel factory and cottage-style workers' houses Consequences: This involvement in Nazi propaganda will color many people's view of the Bauhaus.
Kandinsky writes Schoenberg a long, warm letter; no reply survives. Consequences: Schoenberg's permanent silence

After several years in Paris (retouching photographs, theater sets, painting at night), disgusted by the overly commercial side of the milieu, he settles in the United States and is able to devote himself to painting, apart from a little teaching. Consequences: he discovers Demuth, Dove, Ryder, and Gorky, the first artists to impress him in this country

The start of a long relationship of patronage and friendship: Edlich buys about thirty-five works during the lean years; he is also Kline's family doctor and will attend him during his last illness. about 35 works bought Consequences: allows Kline to survive during the decade before his fame

Elaine graduates in January (midyear graduations were common). Her yearbook photo shows her with downy hair, half demure, half assured, like Barbara Stanwyck. The yearbook tribute: “Elaine the fair, Elaine the lovable, Elaine the lily maid of Brooklyn”. Consequences: Then enrolls at Hunter College.

At the suggestion of Henry Allen Moe, secretary of the Guggenheim Foundation and a friend of the college, Adamic and his wife Stella, a dancer, stop at the college in January 1936 for two or three days; he stays three months. A student: “He was like a sponge, and we water” Consequences: A long magazine article, then a prolonged crisis at the college

An interview with Rice appears in an overly smug tone, disparaging other colleges; Evarts notes in his diary that many were disgusted by it, fearing it would antagonize sensible, well-meaning people. Evarts's diary entry dated January 29, 1936 Consequences: Internal unease among the members of the college

The Yugoslav writer Louis Adamic, famous for The Native's Return (1934) and, like Rice, a former Guggenheim fellow for a year in Europe, arrives with his wife Stella in January 1936 for an afternoon visit suggested by Henry Allen Moe. They stay nearly two months; Adamic falls under the spell of the place and the people, especially Rice, who becomes his friend at once and develops his ideas for him at length. a visit planned for one afternoon; a stay of nearly two months Consequences: the article “Education on a Mountain” for Harper's

On visits to prehistoric sites, little boys hold out pottery fragments through the car window, just as turkeys and goats are sold; the Alberses examine finely formed heads and broken figurines, unable to believe they are holding centuries-old pieces found by peasants while plowing; the archaeologist George Vaillant confirms their authenticity. Words: A woman from a remote region, holding out a small clay head: “Es natural” — it belonged to the soil she knew Atmosphere: Wonder mixed with disbelief, rural trade at the side of the car Stakes: The birth of the collection that will nourish all their work

The Alberses return to the museum again and again; Josef photographs there for whole days; for a few cents they buy heads of little gods dug up by peasants; pottery fragments in their hands, disbelief. Words: Anni: they could not believe that they were holding in their hands centuries-old pre-Columbian pieces found by peasants while plowing Atmosphere: Feverish fascination Stakes: The birth of a collection of more than a thousand objects

Around 11 p.m., the three go out for the first newspaper of the crisis; the usual argument, sharper that evening; Louis, a stammerer who refused to stammer, grated out “the damned fool” (Edward VIII); Rice: “In fact, I envy him”; Stella: “So do I”; Louis, with word-by-word biting courtesy, asks why; Rice: he envies anyone who can love that much Words: Louis: “the damned fool”; Rice: “In fact, I envy him”; Stella: “So do I” Atmosphere: vehemence, a New York night, a stormy friendship Stakes: fidelity to love against reasonable judgment

The usual nighttime outing for the morning paper; that evening's argument, during the abdication crisis, is harsher than usual. Louis, grinding his teeth, wrenches out the words — a stammerer who refuses to stammer — against Edward VIII. The author replies gently that he does not think so; faced with Louis's accusing noise, he goes so far as to say that he envies the king; Stella, before the explosion, lets slip that she does too. Louis, faced with two fools, demands with clipped politeness that they explain; the author envies anyone who can love that much. Words: Louis: “the damned fool”; the author: he envies him; Stella: so does she; Louis, word by word: perhaps they could tell him why, if they please. Atmosphere: nighttime vehemence, a New York newsstand, the winter of the abdication crisis Stakes: a clash between furious public morality and private tenderness

Jonas takes his student to the exhibition and points out that the two best American artists are not in it; Elaine decides to meet them; within two weeks she has met de Kooning and knows she will marry him Words: Jonas: de Kooning and Gorky are the best and are not in the show; Elaine: it took her “about two weeks” Atmosphere: a willful love at first sight, immediate fascination (“mesmerized”) Stakes: the beginning of everything — Elaine's life as an artist

Scene seven of the first part: two figures of movable planes in contrasting colors are manipulated before the audience; forms and colors overlap, and the color intensity varies under the lighting; the scene is at once performance, demonstration, and end-of-course examination. Atmosphere: Playful, optical, theatrical — the audience becomes observer and spectator Stakes: Merging spectator and performer, treating the stage as a total work of art

Four kids playing hooky around a fire; Perry bursts out of a scarlet thicket, his white figure appearing and disappearing between the trunks; the children search for him with their eyes, hampered by the strings of the game between their fingers, and point him out in turn Words: Look, it's Perry Westover training for the race! — Where? Where? I can't see him — There he is! Atmosphere: admiring fright, a fall fire, red flashes Stakes: the old man become a legendary figure in the children's eyes

Rice calls a general meeting in the Lee Hall lobby on institutions that blindly outlive their purposes, then proposes deciding, that very night, to close the college so as to make it unique. Silence; someone hiccups. The debate begins; Rice is ready with every argument and dominates with his powerful voice. The man tortured in his country's prisons rises and launches into a tirade with no direct bearing on the subject. The meeting fizzles out; people get up and mill about; Rice stays seated at the end of the table, smoking his pipe, a tiny log cabin of matches set at his elbow. Words: Rice: institutions outlive their purposes but go on blindly; why not decide, this very evening, to close the college so that it becomes unique among all institutions? Atmosphere: silence, a hiccup, oratorical fever — the moral and emotional equivalent of an old revival meeting; then calm, pipe smoke Stakes: testing the community's attachment to its institution, and revealing Rice's ambivalence toward any attachment

Adamic reads his draft, full of praise for Rice; the discussion turns critical: students dare to say for the first time that Rice is an insensitive Socrates; Zeuch denounces the ghostwriting; Rice admits his heavy-handedness, invites the students to come and tell him their observations, tells them they share the blame for having raised him up by bringing him problems they could handle themselves, and calls on them to see the good side of the article as publicity. Words: Zeuch: Rice practically ghostwrote for Mr. Adamic; it is an open secret. Rice: the students have their share of responsibility for his power. Atmosphere: A rare community tension, criticisms first veiled, then open Stakes: Rice's charisma becomes a community affair; his hunger for recognition revealed

Before they leave, Adamic reads his draft article at a community meeting. The article honors the courageous students and singles out Albers and Wunsch, but above all celebrates Rice, describing him as an idealist-optimist, and compiles the fullest summary to date of his philosophy of education, with long quotations from Rice. “an idealist-optimist: intelligent, well-informed”; publication in Harper's, pp. 519 ff. Consequences: Rice becomes the issue: the college's public hero

Max Weber addresses the congress convened in the face of the disastrous situation in the United States and against fascism abroad: the artist is urged to make connections, and ends up connected with the poorhouse. Weber's remark on the poverty of artists

Even before Gropius's arrival in Cambridge in 1937, Dean Hudnut approaches Albers several times, without agreement. Jill Pearlman argues that Hudnut, although a modernist, did not want to re-create the Bauhaus at the Graduate School of Design and invoked budgetary problems. Hudnut's letters of February 21 and March 23, 1936.

After a first version, Adamic reads his article word for word before the whole community, explaining that it is a journalistic text meant to make the college known, to be revised later for a book. The first part (the Rollins controversy, the founding) is well received; then rumblings: the portrait of Rice as leader and savior (“questions of educational policy were left almost entirely to the leader”), the idealization of the group's influence, people who “die” and are reborn from their former selves. A free and prolonged discussion breaks out after the reading. Adamic: people at BMC “die,” burn with self-contempt, then, “reborn,” rise from the ashes of their former selves Consequences: The meeting turns against Rice, accused of encouraging the idealized vision and of preventing its realization

Joe Martin opens: the college is not as good as Adamic says; his examples are the exception. Evarts: there is malice, too much of it. Hendrickson: the group's influence sometimes stiffens people's defenses. Barber attacks Rice publicly: the group does not know when to stop; after a man has been knocked down, he is left to stew in his own juice; Rice's judgments become the group's property; Rice either deliberately abuses his power or does not realize his strength; there are too many sheep in this place. Nat French confirms: Rice has done harm. Wunsch defends Rice and issues a challenge; Goldenson replies: “We have a rough Socrates here, perhaps we need a little Jesus”. Rice ends with a long confession and a plea for his power to be broken. Rice remains silent during Barber's attack, imperturbably drawing on his pipe Consequences: The debate goes on for weeks, at meals, in the studies, in letters and diaries; most judge the debate beneficial, others are shocked; antagonisms are both clarified and sharpened

DeVoto's attack (Harper's, April 1936) sets off exchanges. Adamic finds the text “a scream”. Gannett, in the Herald-Tribune and then privately, judges a third of DeVoto's remarks to be gross ignorance and recalls Theodore Parker's verdict on Brook Farm: a success for the individuals, a failure as a community. DeVoto replies furiously. Harold H. Anderson (University of Iowa) provides the most brilliant reply, likening DeVoto's hierarchy of intellectual over manual work to choosing between reading a sonnet and taking a bath. Chronology: letters of March 24, March 29, April 6, May 8, 1936 Consequences: A public defense of the college's model

Adamic reads his text word for word, with a preamble on his intentions; the first part goes over well; the rumbling grows over Rice as “top dog and Savior”; total silence until the end of the reading, then a free discussion that turns into a trial of Rice: Martin, Evarts, Hendrickson, then Barber's all-out attack; French confirms; Wunsch counterattacks; Goldenson: a rough Socrates, they need a little Jesus; Adamic challenges Rice; Rice's long confession, pipe in mouth Words: Rice: “The worst sin in the world is impatience, and I am the most impatient person here”; “You should make yourselves into little anti-Rices”; “Rise up so that I'll not amount to anything” Atmosphere: a packed room, tension held in during the reading, an eruption at the end, a whole night of debate Stakes: the community judges its founder, who puts himself on trial

Adamic describes the process by which a student, after the dark night of despair and isolation of his first months, is spiritually reunited with the group. Harper's, April 1936; “The lift of an eyebrow to them is a sentence” Consequences: Serves as the target of the author's criticism and of Bernard De Voto's riposte

Rice is digging potatoes when a student comes up to him: “You're a nice one”. He plays the innocent, learns that Knickerbocker says he has been fired, and suggests she ask to see the Board's letter — whose wording does not amount to a dismissal and leaves open the possibility of improvement. Rice concludes that Knickerbocker has shown himself a liar and that his supporters are abandoning him. Rice's reply, in a tone of acid innocence: “We did? Are you sure?” Consequences: Duberman qualifies: the revolution was not so easy; Knickerbocker and Goldenson announce that they will return in the fall for their year of grace

Adamic's essay makes the college seriously known for the first time: a first encounter with publicity, the beginning of the myth-making. In the following months, the college receives 40 to 50 letters of inquiry a day, and for years applications inspired by the article. 40-50 letters/day Consequences: The BMC myth launched; a flood of applications

Publication in Harper's of a first version of “Black Mountain: An Experiment in Education,” reprinted in 1938 in My America (Harper & Bros.). Harper's, April 1936; book 1938. Consequences: The college enters the lexicon of the educational “experiment”.

The only critical voice outside Black Mountain: DeVoto compares taking part in Black Mountain to Brook Farm, prison, or the army, judges it downright dangerous, resembling a sanatorium for mental illness run by optimistic amateurs. Adamic writes to Rice that DeVoto sums up what is wrong with education and the world. Rice attributes the problem to DeVoto's Utah origins, which made him hate the word community as much as Rice hated the Methodist Church. Harold H. Anderson (University of Iowa) retorts: DeVoto is comparing the incomparable, like asking whether one would rather read a sonnet or take a bath; what laboratory is needed to discover how human beings can live together? Harper's, vol. CLXXII, April 1936, p. 605 Consequences: A national controversy; Adamic's defenders speak up

The Board of Fellows votes to send warnings: to Knickerbocker at the end of his first year of teaching, to Goldenson at the end of his second year — it is quite pessimistic that they can become the kind of teacher wanted here for the long term. Vote: 5 in favor (Rice, Dreier, Mangold, Albers, the student moderator Mary Beaman), 2 against (Georgia, Martin). A 5-2 vote; Georgia's letter to Knickerbocker of April 15, 1936 Consequences: The community polarized; not reappointed in December 1936

Rice is digging potatoes; a student: “You're a nice one”; “What have I done now?”; she informs him that Knickerbocker says he has been fired; Rice feigns surprise and has her ask for the letter — a trap that discredits Knickerbocker in Rice's eyes Words: “You just fired Knickerbocker” — “We did? Are you sure?” Atmosphere: acid irony beneath apparent innocence, in the garden soil Stakes: the battle over the version of events: dismissal or warning?

Three months in Mexico, arriving by car from North Carolina (seven days or more on the road, since Josef disliked flying). A fabulous climate, well-being, and intense output. Josef gained seven pounds (about 3 kg) and painted eleven (or twelve) oil paintings; letter to the Kandinskys of August 22, 1936: Mexico, the promised land of abstract art, which here is thousands of years old Consequences: A constant transformation of both artists' work; Anni creates Escritura antigua and Monte Albán

Josef exhibits graphic work and the series of watercolors Clave de sol at the newspaper El Nacional (August 15-25). He begins abstract linear drawings and paints Arqueológico and Templo, the first studies for Tenayuca. The Alberses meet Diego Rivera. Anni weaves two large wall hangings, Escritura antigua and Monte Albán. Address in Mexico City: calle de París 23; letter to the Kandinskys of August 22, 1936

Exhibition at El Nacional (August 15-25): graphic works and the gouache series Treble Clef; the beginnings of abstract line drawings, the paintings Archaeologic and Temple; the first studies for Tenayuca; a meeting with Diego Rivera. Anni weaves Ancient Writing and Monte Alban. Letters to the Kandinskys (August 22, 1936, Calle de Paris 23): Josef spends whole days photographing at the museum.

A full page of photographs in the Sunday New York Times supplement of June 7, 1936. A member of BMC found it horrible and thoroughly untruthful; the mail received (50-55 letters the first week, about forty the second) often began “Dear Rollins Rebels” or “The Black Mountain Cooperative College”… this is the college of my dreams, especially since it costs nothing. 50-55 letters the first week, ~40 the second Consequences: A misleading public image of the college

Alice applies in the summer of 1936; a faculty member, doubting “if the college could stand another vampire,” votes against her; he is outvoted, and Alice enters in the fall among fifty-five students. 55 students at the start of the 1936 term

Exhibition of Josef's watercolor paintings “Clave de sol” and recent prints, under the auspices of the LEAR (League of Revolutionary Writers and Artists), near the Parque de la Alameda and the Palacio de Bellas Artes (completed in 1934). A front-page article in El Nacional on August 16; Josef hailed as one of the founders of abstractionism. He was expecting negative reviews and was surprised by the reception. Perhaps organized with Porset's help; one of the first exhibitions of his work in the Americas Consequences: Josef discovers that Latin American art is open, eclectic, and receptive to abstraction

Josef's “Treble Clef” gouaches and recent prints shown in the lobby of the headquarters of the left-wing daily El Nacional, 15 Avenida Dr. Mora, along Alameda Park, a stone's throw from the Palacio de Bellas Artes (completed in 1934). Under the patronage of the LEAR (Liga de Escritores y Artistas Revolucionarios); a front-page article in El Nacional on August 16, 1936; a large crowd of intellectuals and artists at the opening; Josef hailed as one of the founders of abstraction. address: 15 Avenida Dr. Mora, alongside Alameda Park Consequences: One of Josef's first exhibitions in the Americas; the radical press publishes long articles; Josef had expected unfavorable reviews

The exhibition, linked to the League of Revolutionary Artists (LEAR), draws a crowd of prominent intellectuals and artists; El Nacional proclaims on its front page of August 16, 1936, that Albers is one of the founders of abstraction, his works being perceived as revolutionary in their complete break with any historical or anecdotal tendency. front-page article in El Nacional, August 16, 1936; “One of the founders of abstraction” Consequences: Josef had expected hostile reviews; a few days later he writes to Kandinsky that the radical press has published long, laudatory articles.

Anni writes to the Kandinskys that she greatly liked Rivera's early frescoes but that he now makes horrible revolutionary illustrations, while finding him powerful and more interesting than his current painting. letters to the Kandinskys, summer 1936

A month earlier, Noguchi had hinted that he might come to work at Black Mountain and make a wall in bas-relief; Rice, Evarts, and Martin, taken with his talent and personality, had met him. Nothing came of it, apparently because of Albers's opposition. Letter from Martin to Mangold, August 31, 1936

Opening of Clave de sol and prints under the auspices of the LEAR, a crowd of artists and intellectuals, a front-page article on August 16, Josef proclaimed a founder of abstractionism Words: Josef to Kandinsky: he had expected negative reviews, but it was quite the opposite Atmosphere: An unexpected triumph in the left-wing press Stakes: Latin American recognition against New York neglect

Josef's gouaches and prints hung in the lobby of the radical newspaper, under the aegis of the LEAR; a large crowd of artists and intellectuals; El Nacional hails him on August 16 as one of the founders of abstraction; Josef, who expected hostility, writes to Kandinsky that the artists were extremely interested Words: Josef to Kandinsky: he expected unfavorable reviews, and it was the reverse (paraphrase) Atmosphere: Post-revolutionary fervor, intense curiosity about abstraction Stakes: The German abstract painter confronts a muralist Mexico he regards as propaganda — and is proved wrong by his own success

Josef, who expected hostile reviews because he despised the socialist murals as propaganda, sees the crowd of intellectuals and artists flock in; El Nacional crowns him on its front page one of the founders of abstraction; the radical press publishes long articles. Words: To Kandinsky: he expected adverse reviews, and it was the reverse: the artists were extremely interested. Atmosphere: Surprise and euphoria after apprehension. Stakes: Abstraction recognized in the land of revolutionary murals.

The pros and cons of admitting a student named “Sweeney” are the subject of a four-page, single-spaced typed letter from Tasker Howard, then on the admissions committee, to the whole committee; John Evarts's diary mentions it in September 1936. four pages, single-spaced

Kocher, still editor of Architectural Record, cites BMC among ten pioneering institutions in design teaching, alongside MIT, Harvard, Cranbrook, Taliesin, and others. Other schools cited: University of Cincinnati, MIT, Michigan, Cranbrook, Taliesin, Minnesota, Harvard, Beaux Arts Institute of Design, NYU; he quotes Albers's essay “Art as Experience” (Progressive Education, Oct. 1935) Consequences: National visibility for the college in architectural circles

The Architectural Record devotes an article to the Education of the Architect and includes Black Mountain in it, although the college has no official architecture program; A. Lawrence Kocher was the magazine's editor, which probably explains the inclusion. The Architectural Record 80.3, p. 212

In the fall of 1936, Rice proposes weekly faculty discussions on teaching; Albers chairs the first, then the chair rotates. Topics: the value of the lecture versus dialogue; the imperialism of teaching; the frontiers and dangers of personalities; deduction versus induction. The faculty, who often attend one another's classes, argue from firsthand information. Exact topics listed; a rotating chair Consequences: One of the few places in higher education where teaching is discussed from the student's perspective as much as the instructor's
Included in New Horizons in American Art; meets the critic Harold Rosenberg

Six weeks after the start of the fall term, the Board of Fellows adopts an unambiguous resolution: Knickerbocker and Goldenson will not be reappointed (Georgia and Martin again dissenting). According to Dreier, Rice stayed in the background, stating his opinion without developing it. Consequences: An eruption of protests

Zeuch, seeing himself as an independent and a lightning rod for discontent, demands an extraordinary faculty meeting with student representatives — Rice and Albers being away on a trip. It goes on late into the night, remarkably frank, and survives in a stenographic record. Zeuch asks why Knickerbocker was fired: this is not an “advance” on other institutions. Knickerbocker says he would prefer to stay. Wunsch explains that he had hoped he would not come back, admired him for coming back, then learned from students, unprompted, that two colleges were forming, one group drifting away from the center; the angry students found support in Knickerbocker. Knickerbocker: isn't that natural? Zeuch: isn't it healthy? Wunsch: not if it is a “union of weakness”. Consequences: The contradictions between the college's proclaimed aims and its actual procedures laid bare

Dreier invites Albers to take part in 4 Painters: six works each by Albers, Dreier, Drewes (a former Bauhaus student), and Kelpe. Albers himself proposes the Addison venue to Sawyer in June 1936; Bartlett Hayes's press release compares abstract art to music. Albers sends six recent paintings; a thin catalog containing Albers's manifesto “Why I Favor Abstract Art”; the local newspaper reproduces the press release almost word for word Consequences: Albers's first public manifesto in favor of abstract art

Some regard any feedback (especially favorable) as flattery; others see it as support. Albers sums up the middle way: as little intervention as possible; the student should be able to say to himself that he has done his work. Rice and Zeuch agree on sparing negative feedback; Rice notes that the most devastating thing with Albers is the brief glance at a piece of work followed by moving on without a word. Zeuch refuses all praise (he never says it is good work); Rice presses him wearily: Zeuch should take Albers's drawing classes and be ignored once in a while. Knickerbocker defends the lecture, which can arouse interest and be an inspiration, citing a Harvard geology professor who made the earth live and tremble on the platform. Meeting of October 19, 1936

Zeuch suggests there is room even for the most bizarre personalities: a disintegrated personality can be a strong personality. Albers: every school has the right to choose personalities suited to its program. Rice tests Zeuch: would he go looking for bad teachers? Zeuch: yes, take one or two. Rice closes: can't he trust the Lord to send them? Meeting of October 12, 1936

The Board of Fellows votes for the first time salaries beyond living expenses, determined on the basis of need, including intangible needs. Rice and Wunsch $2,100 each, Albers $1,700 (second), Georgia $1,300, Joe Martin $300 Consequences: Comparisons and grudges when the amounts become public in June 1937

Rice and Albers away on a trip; Zeuch asks why Knickerbocker was fired, invoking the college's proclaimed superiority; Dreier questions Knickerbocker, who would prefer to stay; Wunsch sets out his conversion: hostile at first, admiring of his return, then alerted by students to the formation of two colleges Words: Zeuch: the dismissal is not an advance; Wunsch: two colleges are forming; Knickerbocker: isn't that natural?; Wunsch: not if it is “a union of weakness” Atmosphere: remarkable frankness, late into the night, a stenographic record Stakes: the gap between the proclaimed ideals and the actual procedures

Two months after his return, Josef writes to Kandinsky: Alfred H. Barr, whom he knew from Germany and who cited his teaching in a footnote of the catalog of Cubism and Abstract Art at MoMA, did not include him in the exhibition; he attributes this to Barr's narrow vision and complains that he has not painted since his return. Remark about poor Barr, who believes only in the works most often reproduced; Josef is 48 in 1936 Consequences: Reveals his wound: securing his place in the annals of painting

Two months after returning from Mexico, Josef writes at length about art in New York and Paris and mentions Cubism and Abstract Art at MoMA; Barr, whom he had met in Germany and who was interested in his teaching (a footnote in the catalog), did not include his work. Josef attributes this to Barr's narrow vision and complains that he has not painted since his return to Black Mountain. 12 paintings made in Mexico, none since the return; age: 48 Consequences: Reveals Josef's ambition and anxiety about his place in the history of painting.

After Thanksgiving 1936, the Board of Fellows votes not to reappoint the two teachers after the current year, with little prompting from Rice. Only Martin and Georgia vote against. Zeuch leads the counterattack, furious above all on Knickerbocker's behalf, and demands a reconsideration at a faculty meeting, where Wunsch explains that information volunteered by students gradually undermined his confidence in Knickerbocker's usefulness. Vote: Martin and Georgia against Consequences: The two teachers leave at the end of the academic year

After Thanksgiving, the Board of Fellows votes not to reappoint Knickerbocker and Goldenson for the following year, with little impetus from Rice; only Martin and Georgia vote against. Consequences: Sets off Zeuch's counterattack and the community crisis

A long meeting at which the Board of Fellows explains its vote: Wunsch accuses Knickerbocker of creating a second college, a group of students anchored against Rice; Knickerbocker defends himself; the two remaining Board members (Martin and Georgia) reveal that they voted against; Zeuch protests against Rice sitting as prosecutor and judge; Goldenson complains that he was never observed in class before his notification. Wunsch had heard as early as September that Knickerbocker was doing well; his information came from students, unsolicited; Dreier and Tasker Howard had spoken to five students Consequences: The internal split deepens; after the Christmas vacation, Zeuch's petition

Before being hired, Knickerbocker says, he warned Rice in Cambridge that he was not a peaceable individual, that he was used to fighting for what he believed in, and that Rice should not invite him if he did not want that kind of person.
About three months after the start of the term, two students elope to get married; the college reacts “pretty calmly; the rector was more upset than anyone else,” according to a staff member.
Albers is invited to give three workshops at Harvard's brand-new Graduate School of Design, whose dean, Joseph Hudnut, is then recruiting Gropius.

“A Second Foreword” (December 1936) and a speech at the BMC luncheon at the Cosmopolitan Club in New York on December 9, 1936 (approx.) repeat the same paragraph on this distinction. two typescripts in the JAAF Archive; one inscribed “written in December 1936”

The president of Sarah Lawrence, Constance Warren, exchanges views with the faculty on administration and curriculum; a delegation from St. John's College debates methods for several days (Willimetz: Rice was never more impressive than in that setting); students and teachers from the Chicago School of Design inspect the art program; among visitors from Antioch, Will Hamlin decides on the spot to transfer after three years in Ohio.

Wunsch explains: facts that came to light gradually after September made him doubtful of Knickerbocker's usefulness; two colleges were supposedly forming, one group drifting away from the center. Knickerbocker retorts that Rice has an extremely destructive effect on personality. Zeuch sets out his doctrine of individual integrity. Tasker Howard turns the accusation around: Knick's warnings blind the students. Wunsch specifies that the problem lies outside the classroom. Anni Albers asks how the two remaining Board members voted: Martin and Georgia admit to having voted against, fearing a club-like college. King compares the Board's decision to Hitler's remilitarization of the Rhineland. Zeuch protests: Rice is sitting as prosecutor and judge of a man he hates — this is the beginning of the end. Schawinsky asks Knickerbocker to set out his method: life is the greatest art. Goldenson concludes: no one visited his classes, he was judged on marginal things — why wasn't the decent thing done? Words: Wunsch: two colleges were forming here; Wunsch: unless it is a union of weakness; Zeuch: the beginning of the end of Black Mountain College; Goldenson: why wasn't the decent thing done? Atmosphere: courtroom tension, a full-scale interrogation, a stenographic record Stakes: the college's identity: a community bound together around a center, or a pluralism of individuals; the fate of two teachers

Jonas notices her in class: she stands out for her look (black trench coat, beret) and for the big book on schizophrenia she carries — perhaps looking for reasons for her mother's behavior She counts on her little blue sweater to get noticed; a brief affair; he takes her to the first exhibition of the American Abstract Artists group Consequences: Jonas introduces her to Willem de Kooning in the fall of 1938

Summer 1937: Anni's mother, Toni Fleischmann, and her father, Siegfried, visit the Alberses in Mexico; Toni keeps a diary of the stay, a major documentary source. Travel diary preserved Consequences: Documentation of the itineraries
Around 1937, Albers photographs the pyramid of Tenayuca, notably the stone serpents encircling its base; the site becomes a recurring motif. print about 25 x 20 cm

Article by Anni Albers published in the college Bulletin (no. 5); reprinted in College Art Journal in January 1944. Black Mountain College Bulletin, 5, 1937; College Art Journal, III, 2, January 1944, pp. 51-54

An opportunity to acquire land and rustic buildings on the other side of the valley: a former summer camp and resort. 676 acres plus some fifty adjoining acres Consequences: The site is named “Lake Eden” and bought
Adamic returns to the college in the fall of 1937.

Minutes of an end-of-year meeting in 1937 on four students (“Cane,” “Carter,” “Norris,” “Somers”) — see the details in the scenes. Consequences: Cane: decision postponed; Carter: sent out into the world; Norris: doubt about his return; Somers: allowed to stay

Knickerbocker's dismissal eventually leads to the departure of about a third of the student body and the faculty — proof, Duberman notes, that he was not without the magnetism Rice denied him. Consequences: A major schism in the college's history
De Kooning works on a commission for a section of a three-part mural titled Medicine
Graham publishes this book, which sparks discussion and establishes his reputation as an intellectual leader among the artists of his generation.

Albers proposes a color workshop: after the previous year's experience, he wants to give more room to practical exercises; each seminar should combine a theoretical introduction followed by the students' practical work, continued as homework if possible.

Drawing on the previous year's experience, Albers proposes to Dean Hudnut more practical exercises: each seminar should begin with a theoretical introduction followed by the students' handwork, extended if possible as homework. Letter to Dean Joseph Hudnut, JAAF archives.

A picnic celebrating Aldous Huxley's visit, photographed: Rice, steel-rimmed glasses on a full face, in animated conversation with Huxley, surrounded by students and trees. photo: Huxley from behind in the foreground
Moholy-Nagy meets Siegel, 24, whose portfolio (photograms, superimpositions, manipulated negatives) illustrates the types of photographic vision in his 1925 book.

The theater teacher Xanti Schawinsky, trained under Oskar Schlemmer at the Bauhaus, creates his piece Spectodrama: abstract costumes of folded paper and colored planes, plays of colored light, movable sets, complex sound effects, theater in the round. folded-paper costumes Consequences: establishes the college's culture of theatrical experiment
An essay on the teaching of crafts: raw material as a training ground for invention; the dual orientation of teaching (models for industry and the work of art). essay dated “1937”

From his first public talks in 1937, at twenty-five, Cage speaks of his influences and of procedures he already calls “experimental”; these texts will be widely published and then collected in 1961 in Silence. the collection Silence (1961) Consequences: Cage's public renown overshadows almost all of BMC's other practices, unlike Albers's writings, which remained largely unpublished
Becomes a United States citizen

Rice replies to Hutchins, who advocated the sincere pursuit of the intellectual virtues and a common stock of fundamental ideas; Rice argues that education must concern itself with what people feel, or else the structure of thought collapses, as in Nazi Germany, where the universities of pure mind remained silent before Hitler article “Fundamentalism and the Higher Learning,” Harper's, 1937; Hutchins, “The Confusion in Higher Education,” 1936
